sk: विज्ञानं यज्ञं तनुते कर्माणि तनुतेऽपि च विज्ञानं देवाः सर्वे ब्रह्म ज्येष्ठमुपासते विज्ञानं ब्रह्म चेद्वेद तस्माच्चेन्न प्रमाद्यति शरीरे पाप्मनो हित्वा सर्वान् कामान् समश्नुत इति तस्माद्वा एतस्माद्विज्ञानमयात् अन्योऽन्तर आत्मा आनन्दमयः तेनैष पूर्णः स वा एष पुरुषविध एव तस्य पुरुषविधताम् अन्वयं पुरुषविधः प्रियमेव शिरः मोदो दक्षिणः पक्षः प्रमोद उत्तरः पक्षः आनन्द आत्मा ब्रह्म पुच्छं प्रतिष्ठा तदप्येष श्लोको भवति ||

hi: विज्ञान (knowledge / discernment / विवेक-ज्ञान) यज्ञ (sacrifice / यज्ञ) को तनुते (extends / spreads / विस्तारित करता है)। कर्माणि (actions / कर्मों को) भी (अपि च) विस्तारित करता है। विज्ञान को (विज्ञानम्) सभी (सर्वे) देवता (gods) ब्रह्म ज्येष्ठम् (as Brahman, the eldest / सर्वश्रेष्ठ ब्रह्म के रूप में) उपासते (worship / उपासना करते हैं)। यदि (चेत्) विज्ञान को ब्रह्म (Brahman) जानता है (वेद) — और यदि (चेत्) उससे (तस्मात्) प्रमाद (negligence / प्रमाद) नहीं करता (न प्रमाद्यति) — तो शरीरे (in the body / शरीर में) पाप्मनः (sins / evils / पापों को) हित्वा (having abandoned / त्याग कर) सर्वान् कामान् (all desires) समश्नुते (attains completely / सम्पूर्ण रूप से प्राप्त करता है)। उस (तस्मात्) इस (एतस्मात्) विज्ञानमय से अन्य (another) अन्तर (inner) आत्मा (self) = आनन्दमय (made of bliss / आनन्द से बना) है। उससे यह पूर्ण (filled) है। वह पुरुषविध (person-shaped) ही है। उसकी पुरुषविधता के अनुसार [यह भी] पुरुषविध है। प्रिय (the dear / प्रिय / pleasure of anticipation) ही (एव) शिर (head)। मोद (delight / मोद / joy of possession) = दक्षिण पक्ष (right wing)। प्रमोद (ecstasy / प्रमोद / supreme delight) = उत्तर पक्ष (left wing)। आनन्द (bliss / आनन्द) = आत्मा (trunk)। ब्रह्म (Brahman) = पुच्छ प्रतिष्ठा (tail-support)। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: Vijñāna (knowledge) extends (tanute) the sacrifice (yajña). It extends actions (karmāṇi) too. All the gods worship vijñāna as Brahman, the eldest (jyeṣṭha). If one knows vijñāna as Brahman and does not become negligent (na pramādyati) therefrom — abandoning (hitvā) sins (pāpman) in the body, one attains (samaśnute) all desires (sarvān kāmān). Other than this [self] made of knowledge, there is an inner self made of bliss (ānandamaya). By that, this [knowledge-self] is filled. That too is person-shaped. Conforming to its person-shape, this [inner self] is also person-shaped. The dear (priya) is its head. Delight (moda) is the right wing. Ecstasy (pramoda) is the left wing. Bliss (ānanda) is the trunk (ātmā). Brahman is the tail-support (puccha-pratiṣṭhā). Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: विस्तारित करता है / extends / spreads
ws.e: extends / spreads / weaves — from √tan (to stretch/extend); vijñāna 'extends' the sacrifice — it gives the ritual its meaning and efficacy; without understanding (vijñāna), ritual action is mechanical

ws.h: प्रमाद करता है / becomes negligent / becomes heedless
ws.e: becomes negligent / heedless — from pra + √mad (to be intoxicated/negligent); the caveat: knowing vijñāna as Brahman is not enough — one must NOT become negligent; knowledge requires sustained attention and practice, not complacency

ws.h: आनन्द से बना / made of bliss
ws.e: made of bliss — ānanda (bliss/joy) + maya (made of); the fifth and innermost kośa — the bliss-sheath; the deepest layer of the person before Brahman itself; characterised by the experience of bliss in deep sleep and in moments of intense joy

ws.h: प्रिय / the dear / pleasure of anticipation
ws.e: the dear / pleasure of anticipation — the happiness felt when one encounters or thinks of a beloved object BEFORE possessing it; the first and mildest degree of joy; the HEAD of the ānandamaya because anticipation initiates all joy

ws.h: मोद / हर्ष / delight / joy of possession
ws.e: delight / joy of possession — the happiness felt when one actually obtains or experiences the desired object; deeper than priya; the second degree of joy

ws.h: प्रमोद / परम हर्ष / ecstasy / supreme delight
ws.e: ecstasy / supreme delight / great rejoicing — pra + moda; the highest intensity of joy — the happiness felt in the full enjoyment of the desired object; the third and most intense degree of experiential joy — yet even this is only a wing, not the trunk

ws.h: आनन्द / परमानन्द / bliss
ws.e: bliss — the trunk/core of the bliss-sheath; deeper than priya, moda, or pramoda — ānanda is not a reaction to an object but the fundamental nature of the Self; it is objectless, causeless bliss — the Self's own nature

gr: The praise of vijñāna and the fifth sheath (ānandamaya): this mantra completes the five-sheath analysis by introducing the innermost kośa — the ānandamaya (bliss-sheath). Part 1 — Praise of vijñāna: vijñāna (knowledge/discernment) is praised as the principle that gives meaning to both sacrifice (yajña) and action (karma). All gods worship vijñāna as Brahman. The caveat: 'na pramādyati' — don't become negligent. Knowledge requires vigilance. Part 2 — The ānandamaya kośa (bliss-sheath): inside the vijñānamaya is the ānandamaya — the self made of bliss (ānanda). Its bird-parts are four degrees of joy: (1) Priya (the dear) = head: the pleasure of anticipation — seeing or thinking of a beloved object. (2) Moda (delight) = right wing: the joy of possession — actually obtaining the desired. (3) Pramoda (ecstasy) = left wing: the supreme delight — fully enjoying the desired. (4) Ānanda (bliss) = trunk: the core — not a reaction to any object but objectless bliss, the Self's own nature. (5) Brahman = tail/support: Brahman is the SUPPORT of the ānandamaya — the ground on which even bliss rests. The critical detail: the pratiṣṭhā (support) of the ānandamaya is BRAHMAN ITSELF — not another principle but the Absolute. This signals that we have reached the innermost boundary — beyond the bliss-sheath is Brahman, the core.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.5.1-2.6.1 — The ānandamaya kośa is the most philosophically debated of the five sheaths. Key question: is the ānandamaya kośa ITSELF Brahman, or is it still a 'sheath' (covering) with Brahman hidden inside it? Shankara says it is still a kośa — the suffix '-maya' means 'made of' (vikāra), not 'full of'; therefore even ānanda (bliss) can be a covering that conceals the Self. Rāmānuja disagrees — he reads '-maya' as 'full of' (prācurya), making the ānandamaya = Brahman full of bliss. The three degrees of joy (priya, moda, pramoda) are traditionally explained as: priya = joy on seeing/anticipating the beloved; moda = joy on obtaining it; pramoda = joy in fully experiencing it. These are experiential, object-dependent joys. Ānanda (the trunk) transcends these — it is the Self's own bliss, independent of objects. The pratiṣṭhā = Brahman is unique — in all previous sheaths, the support was a cosmic element (earth, space, etc.). Here the support is Brahman itself — signalling that we have reached the ultimate ground.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — आनन्दमय = पाँचवाँ कोश (fifth sheath) — अभी भी कोश (still a sheath) — आत्मा (Self) नहीं। '-मय' = विकार (modification) — आनन्दमय = आनन्द का विकार — ब्रह्म स्वयं नहीं। प्रतिष्ठा = ब्रह्म — ब्रह्म = आनन्दमय का आधार (support of the bliss-sheath) = सबसे भीतर = सबसे परे। प्रिय-मोद-प्रमोद = विषय-सुख (object-dependent joy) — आनन्द = निर्विषय (objectless)।
advaita.en: Shankara says ānandamaya = the fifth sheath — still a sheath — NOT the Self. '-Maya' = modification — ānandamaya = a modification of bliss — not Brahman itself. Pratiṣṭhā = Brahman — Brahman = the support of the bliss-sheath = the innermost = the ultimate. Priya-moda-pramoda = object-dependent joy — ānanda = objectless bliss.
advaita.ins: Even bliss is a sheath — the innermost, but still a covering. Priya, moda, pramoda — three intensities of joy, all triggered by objects. But the trunk is ānanda — causeless, objectless bliss. And the support? Brahman itself. We've reached the ground. Peel back bliss, and there is Brahman.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — आनन्दमय = भगवान् स्वयं (God Himself) — '-मय' = 'से परिपूर्ण' (full of) — भगवान् = आनन्द से परिपूर्ण (full of bliss)। आनन्दमय = परब्रह्म (Supreme Brahman) — कोश नहीं। प्रिय-मोद-प्रमोद-आनन्द = भगवान् के आनन्द की चार अभिव्यक्तियाँ (four expressions of God's bliss)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says ānandamaya = God Himself — '-maya' = 'full of' — God = full of bliss. Ānandamaya = the Supreme Brahman — not a sheath. Priya-moda-pramoda-ānanda = four expressions of God's bliss.
vishisht.ins: The innermost self is not a covering but God Himself — full of bliss. Priya, moda, pramoda, ānanda — four intensities of divine joy. God IS bliss, and the ānandamaya IS God. The five-sheath analysis doesn't end with another covering — it ends with the Beloved.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — आनन्दमय = आनन्द-चेतना (bliss-consciousness) — चेतना का सबसे गहन स्तर (deepest plane of consciousness)। प्रिय-मोद-प्रमोद = आनन्द की तीन तरंगें (three waves of bliss) — बाह्य (outer) से आन्तरिक (inner)। आनन्द = चेतना का मूल स्वभाव (fundamental nature of consciousness) = सत्-चित्-आनन्द (Sat-Chit-Ananda) का तीसरा पद।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says ānandamaya = bliss-consciousness — the deepest plane of consciousness. Priya-moda-pramoda = three waves of bliss — from outer to inner. Ānanda = the fundamental nature of consciousness = the third aspect of Sat-Chit-Ananda.
aurobindo.ins: The innermost plane is bliss-consciousness — not bliss as a reaction to something pleasant, but bliss as the very nature of consciousness itself. Three waves — anticipation, possession, full enjoyment — lead to the core: ānanda, causeless, boundless, the Self's own delight in being.

dp.q: 🔍 The three degrees of joy — priya, moda, pramoda
dp.a: The ānandamaya kośa's bird-parts map three degrees of experiential joy plus a fourth that transcends them all: (1) Priya (the dear) = head: the pleasure of ANTICIPATION. When you see something you love, or think of something desired, a wave of happiness arises BEFORE you possess it. This is priya — the joy of recognition, the delight that comes from knowing that what you love exists and is near. Example: seeing food when hungry, seeing a beloved person approaching. (2) Moda (delight) = right wing: the joy of POSSESSION. When you actually obtain the desired object — when you eat the food, when the beloved arrives — a deeper joy arises. This is moda — the satisfaction of having, the pleasure of fulfilment. (3) Pramoda (ecstasy) = left wing: the joy of FULL ENJOYMENT. Beyond mere possession, the total immersion in the experience — the rapture of complete engagement. This is the most intense experiential joy — yet the Taittirīya makes it only a wing, not the core. (4) Ānanda (bliss) = trunk: OBJECTLESS BLISS. Unlike priya, moda, and pramoda, which depend on objects (food, beloved, experiences), ānanda is the Self's own nature — joy without cause, without object, without limit. It is not a reaction but a state of being. The teaching: the three object-dependent joys (priya, moda, pramoda) are pale reflections of the objectless bliss (ānanda) that is the Self's own nature. Every joy you experience in the world is a fragment of the ānanda that IS you.

dp.q: 🔍 The ānandamaya debate — sheath or Self?
dp.a: The ānandamaya kośa has generated one of the most important debates in Indian philosophy: is it a sheath (covering) or is it Brahman itself? Shankara's position (Advaita): the ānandamaya IS a kośa — a covering, not the Self. Arguments: (a) The suffix '-maya' means 'modification of' (vikāra) — just as annamaya means 'made of food' (not food itself), ānandamaya means 'made of bliss' (not bliss itself). (b) It is described with bird-parts (head, wings, trunk, tail) — Brahman, being formless, cannot have parts. (c) It has a pratiṣṭhā (support) — Brahman, being the ultimate ground, cannot rest on anything. BUT: the pratiṣṭhā is Brahman itself — signalling that Brahman is just beyond this last covering. Rāmānuja's position (Viśiṣṭādvaita): the ānandamaya IS Brahman. Arguments: (a) '-Maya' can mean 'full of' (prācurya) — ānandamaya = 'full of bliss' = Brahman. (b) The text says the pratiṣṭhā is Brahman — but so is the ānandamaya. They are the same. (c) The subsequent passage (2.7) identifies Brahman with bliss — confirming that the ānandamaya IS Brahman. The practical resolution: whether the ānandamaya is a sheath or Brahman itself, both schools agree on the experiential teaching: the deepest layer of the person is BLISS. The journey through food, breath, mind, and knowledge ends in joy. The Self's nature is not suffering but delight.

sk: असन्नेव स भवति असद्ब्रह्मेति वेद चेत् अस्ति ब्रह्मेति चेद्वेद सन्तमेनं ततो विदुरिति तस्यैष एव शारीर आत्मा यः पूर्वस्य तत्रैष प्रश्नः किमु विद्वानमुं लोकं प्रेत्य कश्चन गच्छति उ आहो विद्वानमुं लोकं प्रेत्य कश्चित् समश्नुत इति सोऽकामयत बहु स्यां प्रजायेयेति स तपोऽतप्यत स तपस्तप्त्वा इदꣳ सर्वमसृजत यदिदं किञ्च तत्सृष्ट्वा तदेवानुप्राविशत् तदनुप्रविश्य सच्च त्यच्चाभवत् निरुक्तं चानिरुक्तं च निलयनं चानिलयनं च विज्ञानं चाविज्ञानं च सत्यं चानृतं च सत्यमभवत् यदिदं किञ्च तत्सत्यमित्याचक्षते तदप्येष श्लोको भवति ||

hi: असत् (non-existent / अविद्यमान) ही (एव) वह (सः) भवति (becomes / हो जाता है) — यदि (चेत्) 'असत् ब्रह्म' ('Brahman is non-existent / ब्रह्म नहीं है') इति (thus) वेद (knows / जानता है)। [परन्तु] यदि (चेत्) 'अस्ति ब्रह्म' ('Brahman exists / ब्रह्म है') इति वेद — तो (ततः) उसे (एनम्) सन्तम् (as existent / विद्यमान) विदुः (they know / जानते हैं)। उसका (तस्य) = पूर्व (previous / पहले वाले) [कोश] का — यह (एषः) ही शारीर आत्मा (the embodied Self / शरीर-स्थित आत्मा) है। इस विषय में (तत्र) यह (एषः) प्रश्न (question) है: क्या (किम् उ) विद्वान् (the wise) अमुं लोकम् (that world / उस लोक को) प्रेत्य (after departing / मृत्यु के बाद) कोई (कश्चन) गच्छति (goes / जाता है) — अथवा (उ आहो) विद्वान् (the wise) अमुं लोकम् प्रेत्य कोई (कश्चित्) समश्नुते (attains fully / सम्पूर्ण रूप से प्राप्त करता है)? उसने (सः) अकामयत (desired / इच्छा की): 'बहु स्याम् प्रजायेय' ('may I become many, may I be born forth / मैं बहुत हो जाऊँ, मैं प्रजायित हो जाऊँ')। उसने तपः (tapas / austerity) अतप्यत (performed / तपा)। तप कर (तपः तप्त्वा) इदं सर्वम् (this entire universe) असृजत (created / सृजन किया) — जो कुछ भी यह (यत् इदं किञ्च) [है]। उसको (तत्) सृष्ट्वा (having created / सृजन कर) उसी (तत् एव) में अनुप्राविशत् (entered / प्रवेश किया)। उसमें (तत्) अनुप्रविश्य (having entered / प्रवेश कर) सत् (the existent) च (and) त्यत् (the beyond / that) च अभवत् (became / हो गया)। निरुक्त (the defined) च अनिरुक्त (the undefined) च। निलयन (the resting) च अनिलयन (the restless) च। विज्ञान (the conscious) च अविज्ञान (the unconscious) च। सत्य (the true) च अनृत (the untrue) च। सत्यम् (truth / reality) अभवत् (became) — जो कुछ भी यह [है] — उसे (तत्) सत्यम् (satya / truth) इति आचक्षते (they call)। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: He becomes non-existent (asat) indeed if he knows 'Brahman is non-existent.' But if he knows 'Brahman exists (asti)' — then they know him as existent (santa). The Self of the previous [sheath] is the embodied Self (śārīra ātmā) of this one. Here arises this question: does the one who is not wise go to that world after departing? Or does the wise one attain that world after departing? He (Brahman) desired (akāmayata): 'May I become many, may I be born forth (bahu syāṁ prajāyeya).' He performed tapas (austerity). Having performed tapas, He created (asṛjata) all this — whatever there is (yad idaṁ kiñca). Having created it, He entered into it (anuprāviśat). Having entered it, He became the existent (sat) and the beyond (tyat), the defined (nirukta) and the undefined (anirukta), the resting (nilayana) and the restless (anilayana), the conscious (vijñāna) and the unconscious (avijñāna), the true (satya) and the untrue (anṛta). He became truth (satya) — whatever there is — that they call 'satya' (truth/reality). Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: मैं बहुत हो जाऊँ, मैं प्रजायित हो जाऊँ / may I become many, may I be born forth
ws.e: may I become many, may I be born forth — the primordial desire (kāma) of Brahman to become the manifold world; this exact phrase appears in the Chāndogya (6.2.3): 'tad aikṣata bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'It saw: may I become many'; the seed-desire from which all creation springs

ws.h: प्रवेश किया / entered into
ws.e: entered into — anu (after/following) + pra + √viś (to enter); after creating the world, Brahman ENTERED into it — this is the doctrine of divine immanence: God is not separate from creation but pervades it from within; the creator is inside the creation

ws.s: सत् च त्यत् च (sat ca tyat ca)
ws.h: सत् और परे / the existent and the beyond
ws.e: the existent and the beyond — sat (being/existent) + tyat (that/the beyond); Brahman became BOTH the manifest and the unmanifest, the here and the beyond; a series of complementary pairs expressing Brahman's total pervasion of all opposites

ws.h: शरीर-स्थित आत्मा / the embodied Self
ws.e: the embodied Self — śārīra (of/relating to the body/sheath) + ātmā (Self); the Self as it appears within each successive sheath; the ānandamaya is the 'embodied Self' of the vijñānamaya — i.e., the deeper Self that fills and animates the outer sheath

gr: Brahman's creation, entry, and becoming all things: this mantra is one of the most philosophically dense in the Upanishads. The existence question: if one thinks 'Brahman does not exist' (asat), one becomes as if non-existent. If one knows 'Brahman exists' (asti), one is known as existent. Brahman's existence is not an abstract proposition — it determines the knower's own reality. The creation narrative: 'bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'May I become many, may I be born forth.' This primordial desire (kāma) of Brahman is the origin of the universe. Brahman is not compelled to create — it DESIRES to become many, out of its own fullness. Tapas as the creative force: Brahman creates through tapas (creative austerity/heat) — not through labour or material manipulation but through concentrated will-power. The entry (anupraveśa): after creating the world, Brahman ENTERED into it — 'tat eva anuprāviśat.' This is the crucial doctrine of divine immanence: God is not a clockmaker who builds the world and stands apart — God enters the world and becomes it. The pairs of opposites: having entered, Brahman became EVERYTHING — sat and tyat, nirukta and anirukta, nilayana and anilayana, vijñāna and avijñāna, satya and anṛta. Brahman is not just the 'good' half of each pair — it became ALL opposites. This is radical immanence: Brahman is the conscious AND the unconscious, the true AND the untrue. 'Satyam abhavat': the culmination — Brahman became satya (reality/truth). Everything that exists IS satya — IS Brahman. There is nothing that is NOT Brahman.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.6.1 — The phrase 'bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' appears verbatim in the Chāndogya (6.2.3) in Uddālaka's teaching to Śvetaketu — it is one of the most important creation-statements in the Upanishads. The doctrine of anupraveśa (Brahman entering into creation) is central to both Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita — Shankara reads it as Brahman appearing AS creation (vivarta), while Rāmānuja reads it as Brahman literally entering and pervading creation (antaryāmin). The series of complementary pairs (sat-tyat, nirukta-anirukta, etc.) is a comprehensive statement of Brahman's all-pervasiveness — Brahman is not limited to one side of any duality but encompasses both. The claim that Brahman became 'satya and anṛta' (truth and untruth) is philosophically challenging — how can the Absolute include untruth? Shankara handles this by distinguishing absolute truth (pāramārthika satya) from empirical reality (vyāvahārika satya) — at the empirical level, the distinction between true and untrue exists; at the absolute level, even that distinction is Brahman.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'बहु स्याम्' = ब्रह्म का संकल्प (Brahman's will) = सृष्टि का कारण (cause of creation)। 'अनुप्राविशत्' = ब्रह्म ने सृष्टि में प्रवेश = विवर्त (apparent transformation) — ब्रह्म = सृष्टि के रूप में प्रतीत (appears as creation) — जैसे रस्सी = साँप के रूप में। सत्-त्यत् आदि = ब्रह्म = सभी द्वन्द्वों (all pairs of opposites) का अधिष्ठान (substratum)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'bahu syām' = Brahman's will = the cause of creation. 'Anuprāviśat' = Brahman entered creation = vivarta (apparent transformation) — Brahman appears as creation — like a rope appears as a snake. Sat-tyat etc. = Brahman = the substratum of all pairs of opposites.
advaita.ins: Brahman desired: 'May I become many.' It performed tapas. It created everything. Then — the crucial move — it ENTERED what it had created. The creator is inside the creation. It became everything — the defined and undefined, the conscious and unconscious, the true and untrue. There is nothing that is not Brahman.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'बहु स्याम्' = भगवान् की इच्छा (God's will) — सृष्टि = भगवान् की लीला (divine play)। 'अनुप्राविशत्' = भगवान् = अन्तर्यामी (the Inner Controller) — सृष्टि में प्रवेश कर सबका नियमन (control of all from within)। सर्वत्र भगवान् — सत् में भी, असत् में भी।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'bahu syām' = God's will — creation = divine play (līlā). 'Anuprāviśat' = God = the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) — entering creation to control everything from within. God is everywhere — in the existent and in the beyond.
vishisht.ins: God desired to become many — not from need but from fullness, from the joy of creation. He created everything, then entered into everything as the Inner Controller. He became all opposites — the conscious and unconscious, the true and untrue. Nothing exists apart from God.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'बहु स्याम्' = चेतना (consciousness) का आत्म-विस्तार (self-expansion) — एक से अनेक (one becoming many)। 'अनुप्राविशत्' = चेतना = अपनी ही सृष्टि में प्रवेश — सत्-त्यत् = चेतना सभी द्वन्द्वों (pairs of opposites) में स्वयं को अभिव्यक्त करती है — प्रकाश-अन्धकार, ज्ञान-अज्ञान दोनों चेतना के ही रूप।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'bahu syām' = the self-expansion of consciousness — one becoming many. 'Anuprāviśat' = consciousness entering its own creation — sat-tyat = consciousness expresses itself in all pairs of opposites — light-dark, knowledge-ignorance are both forms of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness desired to become many — to express itself in infinite forms. It created through concentrated will (tapas), then entered its own creation. It became everything — conscious and unconscious, defined and undefined. Even what we call 'unconscious matter' is consciousness in a veiled form.

dp.q: 🔍 'Bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — the primordial desire to become many
dp.a: The phrase 'bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' (may I become many, may I be born forth) is the Upanishadic answer to the question 'Why does the universe exist?': The cosmological claim: before creation, Brahman was ONE — undifferentiated, undivided. Then arose a desire (kāma): 'May I become many.' This desire is not born of lack or need — Brahman is already complete (pūrṇa). It is a desire born of FULLNESS — the overflow of being into becoming, the One's spontaneous movement to express itself as the many. The Chāndogya parallel (6.2.3): Uddālaka teaches Śvetaketu: 'sat eva saumya idam agra āsīt, ekam eva advitīyam... tad aikṣata bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'In the beginning, dear one, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. It saw: may I become many, may I be born forth.' The Chāndogya uses 'aikṣata' (saw/willed) instead of the Taittirīya's 'akāmayata' (desired) — both express the same idea: creation arises from conscious intention, not from accident or mechanical necessity. Tapas as creative force: Brahman creates through tapas — concentrated will-power, creative heat. This is not physical labour but the focused energy of consciousness producing reality. The Ṛg Veda (10.129.3) similarly describes creation arising from tapas: 'tapasaḥ tat mahina ajāyata ekam' — 'from the heat of that One, the One was born.' The theological implications: (a) The universe is not an accident — it is WILLED. (b) The universe is not a fall or a mistake — it is a creative expression. (c) The diversity of the world (the 'many') is not opposed to the unity of Brahman (the 'one') — it IS that unity expressing itself.

The statement 'tat sṛṣṭvā tad eva anuprāviśat' (having created that, It entered into that very thing) is one of the most theologically significant claims in the Upanishads — the doctrine of anupraveśa (divine entry/immanence): The claim: Brahman did not merely create the world and stand apart from it. After creating, Brahman ENTERED into the creation. The creator is INSIDE the creation. There is no place, no being, no object that does not contain Brahman within it. The philosophical implications: (a) Divine immanence: God is not separate from the world — God pervades the world from within. Every atom, every being, every moment contains the divine presence. (b) The end of duality: if Brahman has entered into everything, then the distinction between sacred and secular, spiritual and material, divine and mundane collapses. Everything IS Brahman — 'yad idaṁ kiñca' (whatever there is). (c) The basis for 'tat tvam asi': if Brahman has entered into every being, then every being's innermost Self IS Brahman. The Chāndogya's 'tat tvam asi' (you are that) follows logically from the Taittirīya's 'anuprāviśat' (He entered). The pairs of opposites: having entered, Brahman became BOTH sides of every duality: sat-tyat (existent-beyond), nirukta-anirukta (defined-undefined), vijñāna-avijñāna (conscious-unconscious), satya-anṛta (true-untrue). This is total pervasion — Brahman is not only in the light but also in the darkness, not only in knowledge but also in ignorance. Rāmānuja's antaryāmin: Rāmānuja interprets anupraveśa as God becoming the antaryāmin (Inner Controller) — the divine presence that inhabits every being and guides it from within. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.7.1-23) develops this concept in the famous Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa: 'He who dwells in earth, whom earth does not know, whose body earth is, who controls earth from within — He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.'

hi: असत् (non-being / अभाव) ही (वा) यह (इदम्) अग्रे (in the beginning / प्रारम्भ में) आसीत् (was / था)। उससे (ततः) ही (वै) सत् (being / अस्तित्व) अजायत (was born / उत्पन्न हुआ)। उसने (तत्) आत्मानम् (itself / स्वयं को) स्वयम् (by itself / अपने आप) अकुरुत (made / बनाया)। इसलिए (तस्मात्) वह (तत्) सुकृतम् (well-made / self-made / स्व-निर्मित / सुन्दर रचना) उच्यते (is called / कहा जाता है)। जो (यत्) वह सुकृत है — रस (essence / rasa / सार / the flavour of joy) ही (वै) वह (सः) है। रस (essence) को ही (एव) प्राप्त कर (लब्ध्वा) यह [जीव] (अयम्) आनन्दी (blissful / आनन्दित) भवति (becomes / होता है)। कौन (कः) ही (एव) अन्यथा (anyāt / otherwise) प्राण्यात् (would breathe / श्वास लेता) — कौन जीवित रहता — यदि (यत्) यह (एषः) आकाश (space / ether / the space of the heart) में आनन्द (bliss) न (न) होता (स्यात्)? वही (एषः) ही (एव) आनन्दयाति (gives bliss / आनन्दित करता है)। जब (यदा) ही (एव) यह [जीव] (एषः) इस (एतस्मिन्) अदृश्य (invisible), अनात्म्य (bodiless), अनिरुक्त (indefinable), अनिलयन (supportless / without resting place) [ब्रह्म] में अभय (fearless / निर्भय) प्रतिष्ठा (foundation / आधार) विन्दते (finds / पाता है) — तब (अथ) वह (सः) अभयम् गतः (gone to fearlessness / निर्भयता को प्राप्त) भवति (becomes / होता है)। [परन्तु] जब (यदा) यह [जीव] इसमें (एतस्मिन्) उदरम् अन्तरम् (a gap / a hole / एक अन्तर / एक दूरी) कुरुते (makes / बनाता है) — तब (अथ) उसका (तस्य) भय (fear) भवति (arises / उत्पन्न होता है)। वह (तत्) ही (तु एव) भय = विद्वान् (the wise one) का [भी] — [जब वह] अमन्वान (not reflecting properly / ठीक से चिन्तन न करते हुए) [होता है]। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: In the beginning (agre), this was non-being (asat). From that, being (sat) was born. It made itself (ātmānaṁ svayam akuruta) by itself. Therefore it is called 'su-kṛta' (well-made / self-made). That which is su-kṛta — it is rasa (essence/flavour) indeed. For having obtained (labdhvā) that rasa, one becomes blissful (ānandī). Who indeed would breathe (prāṇyāt), who would live, if this bliss (ānanda) were not in space (ākāśa)? For this [Brahman] alone gives bliss (ānandayāti). When one finds a fearless (abhaya) foundation (pratiṣṭhā) in that which is invisible (adṛśya), bodiless (anātmya), indefinable (anirukta), and supportless (anilayana) — then one has gone to fearlessness (abhayam gata). But when one makes even a small gap (udaram antaram) in it — then fear (bhaya) arises. That indeed is fear — even for the wise one who does not reflect properly (amanvāna). Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: सु-निर्मित / स्व-निर्मित / well-made / self-made
ws.e: well-made / self-made — su (well/good) + kṛta (made/done); Brahman is 'su-kṛta' because it made ITSELF — it is self-caused, self-creating; also = 'beautifully made' — creation is a work of beauty and artistry

ws.h: रस / सार / essence / flavour / juice
ws.e: essence / flavour / juice — rasa = the quintessence, the vital sap, the flavour; Brahman is rasa — the distilled essence of all experience; obtaining this rasa makes one ānandī (blissful); cf. the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.4.14): 'vijñānam ānandaṁ brahma... rasaḥ'

ws.h: कौन श्वास लेता / who would breathe
ws.e: who would breathe? — a rhetorical question: if Brahman (as bliss) did not pervade the space of the heart, no one would have the will or energy to breathe or live; life itself is sustained by the underlying bliss of Brahman

ws.h: एक अन्तर / एक दरार / a gap / a split
ws.e: a gap / a split / an interval — udara (belly/cavity) + antara (interval/gap); when the knower perceives even the SMALLEST separation between themselves and Brahman, fear arises; any sense of duality — however subtle — produces fear

ws.h: ठीक से चिन्तन न करते हुए / not reflecting properly
ws.e: not reflecting properly / not meditating correctly — a + manvāna (reflecting/contemplating); even the wise person (viduṣaḥ) experiences fear when they fail to maintain continuous awareness of non-duality; fear is the result of lapses in understanding, not of ignorance alone

gr: Brahman as rasa (essence) and the source of all bliss: this mantra contains some of the Brahmānandavallī's most powerful declarations. 'Asat vā idam agre āsīt': 'In the beginning, this was non-being.' This echoes the Nāsadīya Sūkta (Ṛg Veda 10.129) — the most ancient creation hymn. From non-being, being arose. And it made ITSELF — 'ātmānaṁ svayam akuruta.' Brahman is self-created (su-kṛta). 'Raso vai saḥ': 'That [Brahman] is rasa (essence/flavour).' This is one of the most beautiful definitions of Brahman — Brahman is the distilled ESSENCE of all experience, the 'flavour' that makes life worth living. The rhetorical question: 'ko hyevānyāt kaḥ prāṇyāt' — 'Who indeed would breathe, who would live, if this bliss were not in space?' This declares that BLISS is the sustaining principle of all life. We breathe, we live, we act — because of an underlying bliss that pervades the space of the heart. Without it, no creature would have the impulse to exist. The four negations: Brahman is described as adṛśya (invisible), anātmya (bodiless), anirukta (indefinable), anilayana (without resting place). Yet finding a fearless foundation in this indefinable reality is the goal. The fear principle: 'yadā hyevaiṣa etasminn udaram antaraṁ kurute, atha tasya bhayaṁ bhavati' — when one makes even the SMALLEST gap in one's identification with Brahman, fear arises. Fear = the result of perceived separation from Brahman. Even the wise person fears — when they fail to maintain non-dual awareness.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.7.1 — The opening 'asat vā idam agre āsīt' directly echoes the Nāsadīya Sūkta (Ṛg Veda 10.129.1): 'nāsad āsīn no sad āsīt tadānīm' (there was neither non-being nor being then). Some scholars read 'asat' here not as absolute non-existence but as 'the unmanifest' — Brahman in its unmanifest state before creation. The phrase 'raso vai saḥ' (It is rasa) echoes the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.4.14) where Yājñavalkya describes Brahman as 'vijñānam ānandaṁ brahma... rasaḥ.' The rhetorical question 'ko hyevānyāt kaḥ prāṇyāt' is one of the most quoted lines in the Upanishads — it makes ānanda (bliss) the very ground of existence, not an optional extra. The fear-gap doctrine ('udaram antaraṁ kurute') is psychologically profound: fear is not caused by external threats but by internal SEPARATION — the moment you feel separate from the Absolute, vulnerability arises. This anticipates the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's 'dvitīyād vai bhayaṁ bhavati' (1.4.2) — fear comes from a second.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'रसो वै सः' = ब्रह्म = परम रस (ultimate essence) — सभी आनन्द का स्रोत (source of all joy)। 'कः प्राण्यात्' = आनन्द = जीवन का आधार (basis of life) — बिना आनन्द के कोई जीवित नहीं रहता। 'उदरम् अन्तरम्' = द्वैत-बुद्धि (sense of duality) = भय का कारण (cause of fear)। अभय = अद्वैत-ज्ञान (knowledge of non-duality) = ब्रह्म-तादात्म्य (identity with Brahman)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'raso vai saḥ' = Brahman = the ultimate essence — the source of all joy. 'Ko prāṇyāt' = bliss = the basis of life — without bliss no one would live. 'Udaram antaram' = the sense of duality = the cause of fear. Fearlessness = knowledge of non-duality = identity with Brahman.
advaita.ins: Brahman is rasa — the essence, the flavour that makes everything worth experiencing. Without this underlying bliss, who would breathe? Who would live? Bliss sustains all existence. But the moment you feel separate — even slightly — fear arises. The gap between you and Brahman is where all fear lives.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'रसो वै सः' = भगवान् = सर्व-रस (the essence of all flavours/joys)। 'कः प्राण्यात्' = भगवान् = सबके जीवन का आधार — भगवान् के आनन्द से ही सब जीवित। 'अभयं प्रतिष्ठाम्' = भगवान् में शरणागति (surrender to God) = निर्भयता (fearlessness)। 'उदरम् अन्तरम्' = भगवान् से विमुखता (turning away from God) = भय।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'raso vai saḥ' = God = the essence of all joys. 'Ko prāṇyāt' = God = the basis of all life — all live by God's bliss. 'Abhayaṁ pratiṣṭhām' = surrender to God = fearlessness. 'Udaram antaram' = turning away from God = fear.
vishisht.ins: God is the essence — the rasa — without which nothing has flavour, nothing has meaning. Who would breathe if God's bliss didn't pervade space? Find your foundation in God — invisible, indefinable, yet absolutely real — and fear disappears. The only thing that creates fear is the gap between you and God.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'रसो वै सः' = चेतना का सार (essence of consciousness) = आनन्द — अस्तित्व का मूल स्वाद (fundamental taste of existence)। 'कः प्राण्यात्' = आनन्द = अस्तित्व की प्रेरणा (driving force of existence) — बिना आनन्द के अस्तित्व का कोई कारण नहीं। 'उदरम् अन्तरम्' = चेतना में विभाजन (division in consciousness) = भय।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'raso vai saḥ' = the essence of consciousness = bliss — the fundamental taste of existence. 'Ko prāṇyāt' = bliss = the driving force of existence — without bliss there would be no reason to exist. 'Udaram antaram' = division in consciousness = fear.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness has a taste — and that taste is bliss. Without it, who would want to breathe? Who would bother to live? Bliss is not a reward — it is the very ground of existence. Fear arises only when consciousness divides against itself — when it sees 'other' where there is only Self.

dp.q: 🔍 'Raso vai saḥ' — Brahman as the essence of joy
dp.a: The declaration 'raso vai saḥ' (It/He is rasa indeed) is one of the Upanishads' most evocative definitions of Brahman: What is rasa? Rasa means juice, sap, essence, flavour, taste. It is the distilled quintessence of something — the part that gives it its character, its savour, its value. In aesthetic theory (the later rasa-śāstra of Bharata), rasa = the aesthetic emotion evoked by art. In Āyurveda, rasa = the nutritive essence of food. In the Upanishads, rasa = the essential nature of Brahman — the 'flavour' of reality itself. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka parallel: Yājñavalkya tells Maitreyī (BU 2.4.14): 'vijñānam ānandaṁ brahma... raso vai saḥ' — Brahman is consciousness, bliss, rasa. The Chāndogya (1.1.2-3) also uses rasa in its analysis of OM: 'the essence (rasa) of all beings is earth; the essence of earth is water... the essence of the Sāman is the Udgītha (OM).' Each level distils to an essence; the ultimate essence is Brahman. The existential claim: 'rasaṁ hyevāyaṁ labdhvā ānandī bhavati' — having obtained this rasa, one becomes blissful. The claim is not merely that Brahman is blissful but that Brahman IS the bliss that everyone is already seeking. Every pleasure, every joy, every satisfaction is a taste of this rasa — a fragment of the infinite essence, filtered through finite experience. 'Ko hyevānyāt kaḥ prāṇyāt': 'Who indeed would breathe, who would live, if this ānanda were not in space?' This is the most radical claim: BLISS sustains existence. Not duty, not fear, not survival instinct — bliss. The very will to live comes from the underlying ānanda of Brahman pervading the space of the heart.

dp.q: 🔍 Fear and the gap — 'udaram antaram kurute'
dp.a: The statement 'yadā hyevaiṣa etasminn udaram antaraṁ kurute, atha tasya bhayaṁ bhavati' (when one makes even a small gap in it, then fear arises) offers one of the most psychologically precise analyses of fear in any philosophical text: The mechanism: fear arises from SEPARATION — from perceiving a gap (antara) between yourself and Brahman. As long as there is unity — no gap, no 'other' — there is no fear. The moment duality appears — even the subtlest sense that 'I' am here and 'Brahman' is there — vulnerability arises, and with it, fear. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka's confirmation (1.4.2): 'sa vai naiva reme, tasmād ekākī na ramate... sa dvitīyam aicchat... dvitīyād vai bhayaṁ bhavati' — 'He was not happy; therefore one alone is not happy. He desired a second. Fear comes from a second.' Fear requires a 'second' — an 'other.' No other, no fear. Even the wise person fears: 'tatt veva bhayaṁ viduṣo'manvānasya' — even the knower (viduṣaḥ) fears when not reflecting properly (amanvāna). This is remarkably honest: wisdom is not a permanent state of fearlessness but a practice that requires continuous attention. The wise person CAN slip — and when they do, the gap opens, and fear returns. The practical teaching: (a) Fear is not caused by external threats but by internal separation — the perceived gap between self and Self. (b) Fearlessness comes from finding one's foundation (pratiṣṭhā) in Brahman — invisible, indefinable, supportless, yet absolutely real. (c) This fearlessness requires continuous awareness (manvāna) — even the wise must stay vigilant.

hi: भय (fear / भय) से इसके (अस्मात्) वायु (wind / वातः) बहती (pavate / चलती) है। भय से सूर्य (sun) उदेति (rises / उदय होता है)। भय से अग्नि (fire) और (च) इन्द्र (Indra) और मृत्यु (Death) — पाँचवाँ (पञ्चमः) — धावति (runs / दौड़ता है)। यह (सा एषा) आनन्द की मीमांसा (investigation of bliss / आनन्द की गणना) है: [मान लो] एक युवा (youth) हो — साधु-युवा (a good youth / उत्तम युवक), अध्यायक (learned / विद्यासम्पन्न), आशिष्ठ (swiftest / अत्यन्त शीघ्र), दृढिष्ठ (firmest / अत्यन्त दृढ़), बलिष्ठ (strongest / अत्यन्त बलवान्)। उसकी (तस्य) यह (इयम्) सम्पूर्ण (सर्वा) पृथिवी (earth) धन (vitta / wealth) से पूर्ण (full) हो। वह (सः) एक (एकः) मानुष आनन्द (one unit of human bliss)। उसके सौ-गुना (ते ये शतम्) = एक (एकः) मनुष्यगन्धर्व (human-gandharva) का आनन्द। [इसी प्रकार बढ़ते हुए:] देवगन्धर्व → पितृ-लोक → आजानज-देव → कर्म-देव → देव → इन्द्र → बृहस्पति → प्रजापति → ब्रह्म। वह (सः) एक ब्रह्म का आनन्द (one unit of Brahman's bliss) = श्रोत्रिय (the Vedic scholar) और (च) अकामहत (unsmitted by desires / कामनाओं से अप्रभावित) [पुरुष] का [भी आनन्द]। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: Out of fear (bhīṣā) of It, wind blows (pavate). Out of fear, the sun rises (udeti). Out of fear of It, fire and Indra and Death — the fifth — run (dhāvati). This is the investigation (mīmāṁsā) of bliss (ānanda): Let there be a youth — a good youth (sādhu-yuvā), learned (adhyāyaka), swiftest (āśiṣṭha), firmest (dṛḍhiṣṭha), strongest (baliṣṭha). Let this entire earth be full of wealth (vitta) for him. That is one unit of human bliss (mānuṣa ānanda). A hundred of those = one unit of human-gandharva bliss. [And so ascending:] deva-gandharvas → ancestors (pitṛ) of the long-lasting worlds → gods born of merit (ājānaja) → gods of ritual action (karma-deva) → gods (deva) → Indra → Bṛhaspati → Prajāpati → Brahman. That is one unit of Brahman's bliss — and also [the bliss of] the Vedic scholar (śrotriya) who is unsmitted by desires (akāma-hata). Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: भय से / out of fear
ws.e: out of fear — from bhī (fear); the cosmic forces (wind, sun, fire, Indra, Death) operate in perfect order out of 'fear' of Brahman — i.e., out of obedience to Brahman's law; this 'fear' is not terror but the cosmic order's submission to the supreme principle

ws.h: विचार / गणना / investigation / calculus
ws.e: investigation / calculus / systematic inquiry — from √man (to think); here = the 'calculus of bliss' — a systematic investigation that measures ascending levels of bliss from human to divine to Brahman; the term 'mīmāṁsā' also names one of the six darśanas (philosophical systems)

ws.h: वेद-विद्वान / Vedic scholar / one who has heard the Vedas
ws.e: the Vedic scholar — from śruti (what is heard); one who has studied and mastered the Vedic texts through the oral tradition; the śrotriya represents the ideal of learning

ws.h: कामनाओं से अप्रभावित / unsmitted by desires / free from desire
ws.e: unsmitted by desires — a (not) + kāma (desire) + hata (struck/smitten); one whose consciousness is not disturbed or driven by desires; the crucial qualifier: Brahman's bliss is available to the human who is BOTH learned (śrotriya) AND free from desire (akāma-hata)

gr: The cosmic obedience and the bliss-calculus: this mantra has two parts. Part 1 — Cosmic fear: 'Out of fear of Brahman, wind blows; out of fear, the sun rises; out of fear, fire, Indra, and Death run.' The cosmic forces operate with perfect regularity not from their own power but from obedience to Brahman's order. This 'fear' (bhīṣā) is not terror but cosmic law — the wind doesn't choose when to blow; the sun doesn't decide when to rise. They follow an order that transcends them. This echoes the Kaṭha (2.3.3): 'bhayād asyāgnis tapati, bhayāt tapati sūryaḥ' — 'out of fear of Him, fire burns; out of fear, the sun heats.' Part 2 — The ānanda-mīmāṁsā (bliss-calculus): the Taittirīya constructs a quantitative scale of bliss — from human to divine — each level being 100 times the previous: (1) Human bliss (mānuṣa ānanda) = baseline. (2) Human-gandharva bliss = 100× human. (3) Deva-gandharva = 100× human-gandharva. (4) Pitṛs of long-lasting worlds = 100× deva-gandharva. (5) Born-gods (ājānaja) = 100×. (6) Karma-devas = 100×. (7) Devas = 100×. (8) Indra = 100×. (9) Bṛhaspati = 100×. (10) Prajāpati = 100×. (11) Brahman's bliss = 100× Prajāpati. The punchline: Brahman's bliss = the bliss of the learned scholar (śrotriya) who is free from desire (akāma-hata). The INFINITE bliss of Brahman is available to the human being — not through ascending a cosmic hierarchy but through KNOWLEDGE (śrotriya) and DESIRELESSNESS (akāma-hata).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.8.1 — The 'bhīṣā' verse (cosmic fear) appears in slightly different form in the Kaṭha (2.3.3) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (5.8.1 — in the context of 'akṣara'). The bliss-calculus (ānanda-mīmāṁsā) also appears in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.3.33) with a similar but not identical hierarchy. The baseline unit — the bliss of a perfect youth with all the earth's wealth — establishes that even the MAXIMUM possible human sensory happiness is merely the starting point. The ten levels of escalation (each 100× the previous) mean that Brahman's bliss is 100^10 = 10^20 times human bliss — an inconceivable number, effectively infinite. The crucial identification: 'sa ekaḥ brahmaṇa ānandaḥ — śrotriyasya cākāmahatasya' — Brahman's bliss = the bliss of the desireless scholar. The two qualifications are essential: (a) śrotriya (learned) — knowledge is necessary, not just renunciation; (b) akāma-hata (unsmitted by desire) — freedom from desire is necessary, not just learning. Both together = Brahman-realisation.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'भीषा' = ब्रह्म की सत्ता (authority of Brahman) = विश्व-व्यवस्था (cosmic order) का आधार। आनन्द-मीमांसा = ब्रह्मानन्द (Brahman's bliss) = अनन्त (infinite) — मानवीय सुख = उसका क्षुद्र अंश (infinitesimal fraction)। 'श्रोत्रियस्य अकामहतस्य' = ज्ञान + वैराग्य (knowledge + desirelessness) = ब्रह्मानन्द-प्राप्ति (attainment of Brahman's bliss)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'bhīṣā' = Brahman's authority = the basis of cosmic order. The bliss-calculus: Brahman's bliss = infinite — human happiness = an infinitesimal fraction. 'Śrotriyasya akāmahatasya' = knowledge + desirelessness = attainment of Brahman's bliss.
advaita.ins: Even wind and sun and death obey Brahman's order — out of awe, out of the law that governs everything. And Brahman's bliss? Take the happiest human imaginable — young, learned, strong, owning all the earth's wealth. Multiply that joy by 100, ten times over. That's Brahman's bliss. And it's available to the scholar who is free from desire.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'भीषा' = भगवान् का ऐश्वर्य (God's sovereignty) — सृष्टि = भगवान् की आज्ञा (God's command) से चलती है। आनन्द-मीमांसा = भगवान् का आनन्द = अनन्त (infinite) — सबसे ऊपर। 'श्रोत्रिय + अकामहत' = भक्त (devotee) जो ज्ञानवान् + निष्काम (learned + desireless) = भगवद्-आनन्द (God's bliss) प्राप्त।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'bhīṣā' = God's sovereignty — creation operates by God's command. The bliss-calculus: God's bliss = infinite — above all. 'Śrotriya + akāmahata' = the devotee who is learned + desireless = attains God's bliss.
vishisht.ins: The wind blows because God commands. The sun rises because God wills. Even Death runs at His order. And God's bliss — beyond all hierarchy of beings, beyond gandharvas and gods and Prajāpati — that infinite bliss is available to the devotee who is learned and free from desire.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'भीषा' = ब्रह्म-चेतना (Brahman-consciousness) = सब शक्तियों (powers) को नियन्त्रित (controls) करने वाली। आनन्द-मीमांसा = आनन्द का उत्तरोत्तर स्केल (ascending scale of bliss) = चेतना के स्तरों (levels of consciousness) से सम्बद्ध। ब्रह्मानन्द = शुद्ध सच्चिदानन्द (pure Sat-Chit-Ananda) = सर्वोच्च चेतना-स्तर का आनन्द।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'bhīṣā' = Brahman-consciousness controls all cosmic powers. The bliss-calculus = an ascending scale of bliss corresponding to levels of consciousness. Brahman's bliss = pure Sat-Chit-Ananda = the bliss of the highest plane of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The cosmic forces obey Brahman — not from terror but from the inherent order of consciousness. And the bliss-calculus shows that each higher plane of consciousness carries exponentially greater joy. At the summit: Brahman's bliss — pure, infinite, the source of all lesser joys. And it's not reserved for gods — it belongs to the human who knows and is free.

dp.q: 🔍 The ānanda-mīmāṁsā — the calculus of bliss
dp.a: The ānanda-mīmāṁsā (investigation/calculus of bliss) is one of the most famous passages in the Upanishads — a systematic escalation of joy from human to divine: The baseline: imagine the HAPPIEST possible human — young, healthy, good, learned, vigorous, strong, AND possessing all the wealth of the entire earth. His happiness = one unit of human bliss (mānuṣa ānanda). The escalation: 100 units of human bliss = 1 unit of human-gandharva bliss. 100 of those = 1 deva-gandharva. And so on through: ancestors → born-gods → karma-gods → gods → Indra → Bṛhaspati → Prajāpati → Brahman. Each step = 100× the previous. The mathematics: 10 steps of 100× = 100^10 = 10^20 (one hundred quintillion) times human bliss. This is the Upanishad's way of saying: Brahman's bliss is INFINITE — so far beyond human experience that even an astronomical multiplier barely gestures at it. The punchline: 'sa ekaḥ brahmaṇa ānandaḥ — śrotriyasya cākāmahatasya.' One unit of Brahman's bliss = the bliss of the learned, desireless scholar. The 10^20-fold bliss isn't reserved for celestial beings — it is available RIGHT HERE to the human who meets two conditions: (a) LEARNING (śrotriya) — you must KNOW; (b) DESIRELESSNESS (akāma-hata) — you must be free from the craving that fragments experience. The teaching: every human pleasure is a fragment of Brahman's bliss, filtered through desire and limitation. Remove the filter (desire) and add the lens (knowledge), and the full bliss of Brahman becomes your own.

dp.q: 🔍 'Śrotriyasya cākāmahatasya' — the two conditions for infinite bliss
dp.a: The qualifier 'śrotriyasya cākāmahatasya' (of the Vedic scholar who is unsmitted by desires) specifies the TWO conditions for experiencing Brahman's bliss in a human life: (1) Śrotriya (the learned one): from śruti (what is heard) — one who has received, studied, and absorbed the Vedic teachings through the traditional oral transmission. This represents KNOWLEDGE — not casual acquaintance but deep, systematic understanding of the nature of reality as taught in the Upanishads. Without knowledge, one cannot recognise Brahman even when experiencing it. (2) Akāma-hata (unsmitted by desires): a (not) + kāma (desire) + hata (struck/smitten). Not 'without desires' in the sense of deadness or indifference, but 'not driven/controlled by desires.' The normal human experiences bliss in fragments — a taste here, a moment there — because desire divides experience into wanting, getting, and losing. Each fragment of joy is followed by desire for more. The akāma-hata person has transcended this cycle — they experience bliss directly, without the intermediary of desire. Both are necessary: (a) Knowledge without desirelessness = intellectual understanding that doesn't transform. The scholar who knows 'Brahman is bliss' but is still driven by desires knows the fact but doesn't experience the bliss. (b) Desirelessness without knowledge = a calm emptiness that doesn't know what it is. The person who has overcome desires but lacks understanding may be peaceful but doesn't recognise their peace as Brahman's bliss. (c) BOTH together = the bliss of Brahman experienced in a human body. Knowledge identifies it; desirelessness removes the obstacles to experiencing it fully. The radical equality: the Taittirīya equates the bliss of Brahman (the cosmic Absolute) with the bliss of a HUMAN BEING who meets these two conditions. This means: you don't have to become a god, a gandharva, or Prajāpati to experience infinite bliss. You have to KNOW and be FREE.
